opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that it shouldn't be a fixed split. It should follow who bears the cost of a decision and who has the information to make it well.

In practice, the algorithm side usually decides *what* the model should be: the architecture, the attention variant, how many experts, the context length they want to support. They're closest to the quality signal, and they're the ones who know whether a change actually makes the model smarter. The infrastructure side owns *how* it runs: kernels, parallelism strategy, memory management, scheduling, how it behaves under real traffic.

The problem is that this clean boundary is mostly a fiction now. Many architecture choices are really systems choices in disguise. The number of KV heads, whether you use MLA-style compression, how big the experts are, how routing is balanced: each of these can change your serving cost by a large factor. If the algorithm team decides alone, you can end up with a model that's a bit better on benchmarks but two or three times more expensive to serve, and nobody signed off on that trade. On the other hand, if infra has veto power over everything, you get a very conservative model that's easy to run and not very interesting.

So what I've seen work is three things.

First, put infra people in the room early, at the design stage, not after the checkpoint is done. Once the weights are trained, the cost structure is basically locked in, and infra can only polish it.

Second, make the trade-offs explicit and measurable. Don't argue "this is elegant" against "this is hard to implement." Argue "this gains this much quality, and it costs this much in throughput or latency at our target batch size." When both sides share one cost model, a lot of the politics goes away.

Third, the final call on a trade-off should sit with someone who owns the end-to-end outcome, whether that's the product or the cost per token, not with either team alone. Each team naturally optimizes its own metric, so somebody has to be accountable for the sum.

From the open-source side, working on inference engines, we feel this a lot. A new model drops with some novel architectural trick, and the whole community scrambles to support it efficiently. Sometimes a tiny change on the modeling side, which took the researchers an afternoon, would have saved weeks of kernel work. That asymmetry is the strongest argument for co-design: a decision that is cheap on one side can be very expensive on the other, and you only see that if the two sides actually talk.

r001.rationale: The response assigns model choices to the algorithm side and implementation choices to infrastructure, but does not say algorithm teams have greater decision-making authority in many companies.

r002.rationale: It explicitly argues for co-design, with infrastructure involved early and decisions made using shared trade-offs and end-to-end accountability.

r003.rationale: It says infrastructure options become limited after model weights are trained, but does not explain that hardware dominates co-design because the hardware has already been designed.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because in my experience the friction between algorithm and infrastructure teams is rarely about technical disagreement. It's about who gets to decide, and when.

My basic view is that authority should follow the cost of being wrong. When an algorithm researcher wants to try a new attention variant or a new parallelism scheme, the cost of a failed experiment is a few days of compute. That decision should sit with them, and infrastructure should make it as cheap as possible to try. But when a decision shapes the whole stack — the training framework, the communication library, the inference engine everyone depends on — a wrong call costs months and affects every team. Those decisions need infrastructure people at the table with real veto power, not just a service role.

The failure mode I see most often is treating infrastructure as a ticket queue. Researchers decide what they want, throw it over the wall, and the infra team scrambles to make it work. That produces two bad outcomes. First, researchers make choices without understanding hardware constraints, so you get models that are elegant on paper and miserable to serve. Second, infra engineers lose any sense of ownership and start optimizing for not being blamed rather than for making the system good.

What has worked better, at least in the projects I've been part of, is making the boundary itself a shared design object. Agree together on what the interface is — what the model code is allowed to assume, what the runtime promises — and then each side has full authority inside its own territory. Algorithm people can change anything above the line without asking. Infra people can refactor anything below the line without asking. The only things that require joint decision are changes to the line.

The other thing I'd say is that the best people I've worked with refuse to stay on one side. The researchers who understand memory bandwidth and the infra engineers who read the paper before building the kernel end up making most of the important calls, regardless of their official role. So rather than drawing a sharp organizational line, I'd rather invest in people who can cross it. The sharing of authority then happens naturally, because the person making the decision actually understands both sides of the tradeoff.

r001.rationale: The response assigns authority according to the cost of a mistake and describes shared or separate decision rights; it does not say algorithm teams have more authority in many companies.

r002.rationale: It recommends that teams jointly design the boundary between model code and runtime, with joint decisions when that boundary changes, and describes this as what has worked better.

r003.rationale: It mentions hardware constraints and memory bandwidth, but does not say hardware dominates co-design in practice because it has already been designed.

astra-6.text:
I think authority should follow expertise, but the goals need to be shared. The algorithm team should lead on what the model needs to achieve and how to measure its quality. The infrastructure team should lead on how to run it reliably and efficiently, including deployment, resource management, and operational constraints.

The difficult decisions sit between those areas. If an algorithm change improves quality but doubles serving cost, neither team should make that decision alone. They need to look at the same measurements and agree on whether the improvement is worth the cost for the user.

So I’d give each team clear ownership, with joint decisions where the tradeoffs cross that boundary. And I’d involve infrastructure early, while the algorithm is still being designed. That gives both teams a chance to shape a solution that actually works in production.

r001.rationale: The response assigns each team authority within its area of expertise but does not say algorithm teams have more authority in many companies.

r002.rationale: It recommends involving infrastructure early in algorithm design and making cross-boundary tradeoffs jointly, which communicates co-design.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss hardware dominating co-design in practice or explain that this is because hardware is already designed.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the decision-making authority should follow the expertise, but also the consequences of the decision. The algorithm team should lead on model behavior, training objectives, and what quality means for the application. The infrastructure team should lead on system architecture, reliability, and how to operate within the available hardware and budget.

But many important decisions sit between those two areas. If you change the model architecture, that can have a huge impact on inference cost. If you change the numerical precision, that can affect model quality. Neither team should make those decisions in isolation. They should agree on the constraints and run experiments together.

For me, the key is to have a shared objective—say, achieving a certain quality under a latency and cost budget—and a clear owner for each decision. You want both teams to understand the tradeoffs, without requiring everyone to approve everything.

r001.rationale: It assigns decision areas by expertise but does not say algorithm teams have more authority in many companies.

r002.rationale: It says decisions spanning both areas should not be made in isolation and calls for agreeing on constraints and running experiments together.

r003.rationale: It discusses available hardware and budget but does not explain that hardware tends to dominate co-design because it is already designed.
